title: Scala tutorial: pattern matching, collections, case classes and Option — cv.cm
description: Learn Scala 3 step by step: run Hello, world, val and var, if and for expressions, pattern matching, functions, immutable collections, case classes and Option.
answer: Scala is a statically typed JVM language that combines object-oriented and functional programming, used widely for data engineering with Apache Spark and for concurrent backends. Its key features are type inference, immutable collections, case classes and pattern matching. This page uses Scala 3 to cover setup, values, control flow, functions, collections, traits, enums and error handling with Option, Either and Try.

sections.h: What Scala is and what it is used for
body: Scala is a statically typed language that combines object-oriented and functional programming. It was created by Martin Odersky at EPFL and runs mainly on the Java Virtual Machine, with Scala.js for the browser and Scala Native for native binaries. Scala code can use any Java library.

Scala is widely used for data engineering (Apache Spark is written in Scala), for concurrent and distributed backends (Akka, Pekko, ZIO, Cats Effect), and for financial and streaming systems. This tutorial uses Scala 3 syntax, which allows indentation-based blocks; braces still work.

sections.h: Install Scala and run Hello, world
body: The recommended installer is Coursier (`cs setup`), which installs the `scala` command and a JDK. In Scala 3, a method annotated with `@main` is a program entry point.
For larger projects, sbt and Mill are the common build tools. Scastie (scastie.scala-lang.org) runs Scala in the browser without installing anything.
Use `val` for an immutable value and `var` for a mutable variable. Types are inferred but can be written after a colon. Idiomatic Scala uses `val` almost everywhere.

body.code:
val name = "Scala"            // String
var count: Int = 1            // mutable
count += 1
val ratio = 3.0 / 4           // Double: 0.75
val big = 12345678901L        // Long
val ok = count > 1            // Boolean
println(s"$name: count=$count ratio=$ratio ok=$ok")
// Scala: count=2 ratio=0.75 ok=true
println(f"pi is ${math.Pi}%.3f")   // pi is 3.142

body: Everything in Scala is an expression: `if`, blocks and `match` all return a value, so you rarely need temporary `var`s.
`if` returns a value. `for` loops over ranges and collections, and with `yield` it builds a new collection. `match` is Scala's powerful pattern matching, a signature feature of the language.

body.code:
val n = 7
val parity = if n % 2 == 0 then "even" else "odd"
println(parity)                        // odd
for i <- 1 to 3 do print(s"$i ")       // 1 2 3
println()
val squares = for i <- 1 to 4 yield i * i
println(squares)                       // Vector(1, 4, 9, 16)
def describe(x: Any): String = x match
  case 0             => "zero"
  case i: Int if i < 0 => "negative int"
  case i: Int        => s"int $i"
  case s: String     => s"string of length ${s.length}"
  case (a, b)        => s"pair $a and $b"
  case _             => "something else"
println(describe(-5))                  // negative int
println(describe("hey"))               // string of length 3
println(describe((1, "x")))            // pair 1 and x

body: `1 to 3` includes 3; `1 until 3` stops before 3. The final `case _` is a wildcard that matches anything; without it, an unmatched value throws a `MatchError`.
Methods are defined with `def`. Functions are values: you can store them, pass them as arguments and return them. Parameters can have default values, and callers can use named arguments.

body.code:
def add(a: Int, b: Int): Int = a + b
def greet(name: String, greeting: String = "Hello"): String =
  s"$greeting, $name!"
val double = (x: Int) => x * 2        // function value
def applyTwice(f: Int => Int, x: Int): Int = f(f(x))
println(add(2, 3))                    // 5
println(greet("Ann"))                 // Hello, Ann!
println(greet("Ann", greeting = "Hi")) // Hi, Ann!
println(applyTwice(double, 5))        // 20
println(List(1, 2, 3, 4).filter(_ % 2 == 0).map(_ * 10)) // List(20, 40)

body: The underscore in `_ * 10` is shorthand for a one-parameter lambda, `x => x * 10`.

The standard collections are immutable by default: operations such as `map`, `filter` and `:+` return a new collection and leave the original unchanged. Mutable versions live in `scala.collection.mutable`.

body.code:
val nums = List(5, 3, 8)
val more = nums :+ 1                  // List(5, 3, 8, 1); nums unchanged
println(more.sorted)                  // List(1, 3, 5, 8)
println(nums.sum)                     // 16
val v = Vector("a", "b", "c")         // fast indexed access
println(v(1))                         // b
val ages = Map("Ann" -> 31, "Bo" -> 25)
println(ages("Ann"))                  // 31
println(ages.get("Zed"))              // None
println(ages.getOrElse("Zed", 0))     // 0
val unique = Set(1, 2, 2, 3)
println(unique.size)                  // 3
val words = List("apple", "avocado", "banana")
println(words.groupBy(_.head)('a'))  // List(apple, avocado)

head: Collection
Use it for
rows: immutable linked list; fast prepend and head/tail access
immutable indexed sequence; good general default

body: A `case class` is an immutable data type that automatically gets equality, `toString`, `copy` and pattern-matching support. A `trait` is like an interface that can also contain code. Scala 3 adds `enum` for algebraic data types.

body.code:
trait Shape:
  def area: Double
case class Circle(r: Double) extends Shape:
  def area: Double = math.Pi * r * r
case class Rect(w: Double, h: Double) extends Shape:
  def area: Double = w * h
enum Color:
  case Red, Green, Blue
@main def shapes(): Unit =
  val all: List[Shape] = List(Circle(1), Rect(2, 3))
  all.foreach(s => println(f"$s area=${s.area}%.2f"))
  // Circle(1.0) area=3.14
  // Rect(2.0,3.0) area=6.00
  val r = Rect(2, 3)
  println(r == Rect(2, 3))            // true
  println(r.copy(h = 10))             // Rect(2.0,10.0)
  println(Color.values.toList)        // List(Red, Green, Blue)

body: Other signature features include `given` and `using` (contextual parameters, formerly implicits), extension methods, opaque types and union types such as `Int | String`.

sections.h: Error handling with Option, Either and Try
body: Scala supports `try`, `catch` and `finally`, but idiomatic code models failure with types. `Option` is either `Some(value)` or `None`; `Either` holds a `Left` error or a `Right` result; `Try` captures an exception as `Failure`.

body.note: Avoid `null` in Scala code and avoid calling `.get` on an `Option`, which throws if it is `None`. Use `getOrElse`, `map`, `match` or a `for` comprehension instead.

sections.h: A small complete program: grade report
body: This program parses lines of `name,score`, skips invalid lines and prints each student's average. It uses case classes, `Option`, `groupBy` and string formatting.

body.note: Common beginner mistakes: mixing tabs and inconsistent indentation in Scala 3 indentation syntax; integer division (`3 / 4` is `0`, write `3.0 / 4`); using `var` and mutable collections by habit; calling `.get` on `Option`; and writing non-exhaustive `match` expressions.

The Scala Toolkit for everyday tasks such as files, JSON and HTTP.
The Apache Spark documentation if you want to use Scala for data processing.

faq.q: Should I learn Scala 2 or Scala 3?
faq.a: Learn Scala 3 for new projects. Scala 2.13 is still found in many existing codebases, including parts of the Spark ecosystem, and most core concepts are the same.
Scala is both object-oriented and functional. Every value is an object, but functions are first-class values, collections are immutable by default and pattern matching is central.

faq.q: What is the difference between val and var in Scala?
faq.a: `val` defines a value that cannot be reassigned, and `var` defines a variable that can. Idiomatic Scala prefers `val` together with immutable collections.
A case class is a class meant for immutable data. The compiler generates structural equality, a readable `toString`, a `copy` method and support for pattern matching.
Yes. It remains a core language for Apache Spark, for streaming and data platforms, and for functional backend libraries such as ZIO and Cats Effect.
